intended_object: Take a short exact sequence of modules 0 → A → B → C → 0, a basis (a_i) of A, a basis (c_j) of C and any lifts s_j ∈ B with g(s_j) = c_j. Then the family (f(a_i)) ⊔ (s_j), indexed by κ ⊕ σ, is a basis of B. This is the standard construction behind Reidemeister/Milnor torsion. I inferred it from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The definition takes the product basis a.prod c of A × C. It then transports it to B through the inverse of an isomorphism B ≃ A × C. That isomorphism is obtained from `Function.Exact.splitSurjectiveEquiv`, using the section C → B defined by `c.constr ℕ s`, which sends c_j to s_j.

The lemmas `ofExactLift_inl` and `ofExactLift_inr` show that the resulting basis is f(a i) on the left summand and s j on the right summand, exactly as described. The construction is the textbook one.

The setting is fully general: a semiring R, with additive commutative groups because exactness and the splitting require subtraction. No commutativity, finiteness or field hypotheses are imposed; the later determinant results add commutativity only where they need it.

Mathlib's `ModuleCat.Basis.ofShortExact` and `Module.Basis.sumQuot` build related bases, but each fixes one choice of lifts through `surjInv`. This definition allows arbitrary lifts, which is the point of the file and what the determinant results need. So Mathlib has no more general version of the same object.

Surjectivity of g is not assumed explicitly. It follows from the fact that the basis vectors c_j have preimages s_j, so it is not a missing condition.
